articles.title: ESA's Hera Mission Targets Binary Asteroid Pair in November
articles.description: In just one more month, the European Space Agency’s Hera mission will make history. Moving at 12 kilometers per second versus Earth, the mission is about to rendezvous with the binary Dimorphos-Didymos asteroid pair. NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission slammed into Dimorphos in 2022, and now Hera will provide a follow up view of the mission’s resulting handiwork. The European Space Agency (ESA) recently released a thought-provoking look at the perspectives of Hera, and what an astronaut might see from the surface of the asteroids as the mission speeds by.
articles.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera mission will make history in November by targeting a binary asteroid pair at 12 kilometers per second. This landmark planetary defense mission represents humanity's first intentional asteroid deflection follow-up.

articles.title: Webb spots possible early-universe supernova just days after it happened
articles.description: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has detected a possible supernova in the early universe just days after the star exploded. Called AT 2026abck, the transient lies in a star-forming galaxy at a redshift of 5.017 and was found without the help of gravitational lensing. JWST observations suggest the event was caught only about four to 10 days after the explosion. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 29.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has detected a possible supernova in the early universe just days after the explosion, achieving remarkable observational speed.

articles.title: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
articles.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.
articles.summary: James Webb Space Telescope reveals an unexpectedly massive and dense ancient galaxy cluster that challenges current models of early universe structure.

articles.title: Artemis-2-Mission: Nasa veröffentlicht 800 Gigabyte Daten für alle
articles.description:
Die Nasa veröffentlicht in dieser Woche einen riesigen Datensatz der Artemis-2-Mission. Warum die mehr als 800 Gigabyte an Mond-Daten so besonders sind.
weiterlesen auf t3n.de
articles.summary: NASA releases over 800 gigabytes of comprehensive data from the Artemis II mission, making unprecedented mission information publicly available for scientific analysis and discovery.

articles.title: Artemis II : la NASA dévoile plus de 11 000 photos et vidéos inédites de la mission
articles.description: La NASA publie environ 800 Go de données relatives à la mission Artemis II. Au programme : des milliers de photos et vidéos, 8h30 de sons, des images annotées par...
articles.summary: NASA unveils approximately 800 GB of Artemis II mission data including over 11,000 new photos and videos, providing an unprecedented window into humanity's return to lunar exploration.

articles.title: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
articles.description: If you thought you’d seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission, you’re wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and…
articles.summary: NASA publicly releases over 800 gigabytes of Artemis II mission data online, offering the global community unprecedented access to comprehensive imagery and information from the landmark lunar mission.

articles.title: Mars moon lander set to launch on 19 October
articles.description:
The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is set to launch into space on a H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center at 04:41 JST on 20 October 2026 (20:41 BST / 21:41 CEST on 19 October 2026). MMX will be the first mission to collect a sample from Mars’s moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth. 
MMX is led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), in collaboration with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the French space agency (CNES), the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and the European Space Agency (ESA).
articles.summary: Japan's Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is set to launch on October 19, targeting the moons of Mars aboard an H3 rocket. This landmark mission will explore one of the solar system's least understood celestial bodies.

articles.title: Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks
articles.description: The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.
articles.summary: The ESA's Solar Orbiter has directly observed mysterious magnetic switchbacks in the Sun's atmosphere, advancing our understanding of solar physics. These S-shaped kinks provide crucial insights into solar wind dynamics.

articles.title: Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.description:
Image:
			Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope captures spectacular stellar jets erupting from a nebula with extraordinary detail. This observation reveals the dynamic processes of star formation and energetic outflows.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to begin operations on September 23, studying Earth's magnetosphere interactions. This collaborative effort promises breakthrough discoveries in space weather science.

articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals galaxies in unprecedented detail through gravitational lensing effects. This cosmic magnification allows astronomers to observe distant galaxies with remarkable clarity.

articles.title: New Data from the Juno Spacecraft Reveals that Jupiter's Has a Rippling, Wavy Magnetodisk
articles.description: Using observations from NASA's Juno spacecraft, an international team led by Shandong University shows that Jupiter's magnetodisk is a rippling structure that rotates with the planet, contrary to what scientists previously thought.
articles.summary: NASA's Juno spacecraft reveals that Jupiter's magnetodisk has a rippling, wavy structure previously unknown to scientists. This discovery fundamentally changes our understanding of gas giant magnetospheres.

articles.title: Primordial Helium Further Confirms Our Understanding Of The Big Bang
articles.description: Most helium in the Universe is primordial helium, formed during the Big Bang. But a fraction of helium was formed by long-dead stars. Distinguishing between the two allows astronomers to further confirm our observations of the Big Bang.
articles.summary: Primordial helium observations further validate our understanding of Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the universe's earliest moments. This confirmation strengthens the foundation of modern cosmological theory.

articles.title: NASA JPL testing readies Voyager technologies lander for moon mission
articles.description: A commercial lander that will be at the forefront of NASA's efforts to establish a moon base, humanity's first lunar outpost, has passed a series of critical tests at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The tests simulated the extreme temperatures and vacuum of space, as well as the intense shaking and ear-splitting roar of launch. Results show that Voyager Technologies' Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) spacecraft is ready to survive the rigors of space exploration.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA JPL is testing advanced Voyager-derived technologies for a commercial lander that will support humanity's first permanent lunar base.

articles.title: Planetary systems reveal two distinct families tied to their host stars
articles.description: Analyzing a sample of 300 of the best-characterized planetary systems among the more than 1,000 known in the Milky Way, an international research team led by the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF) has discovered that the multiplanet systems identified so far belong to two distinct "families."
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Analysis of 300 characterized planetary systems reveals two distinct families of planets organized by their relationship to host stars.

articles.title: Vera Rubin Observatory spots the largest ultra-fast spinning asteroid yet
articles.description: The speed of an asteroid's spin can tell astronomers a surprising amount about what it is made of. However, existing approaches to measuring spin based on telescope observations can often produce misleading estimates.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The Vera Rubin Observatory has identified the largest ultra-fast spinning asteroid ever detected, providing insights into asteroid composition and formation.

articles.title: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants may be finely balanced to make life possible. Even tiny changes to these constants could make liquids too thick or too thin for essential biological processes, potentially preventing life as we know it. Surprisingly, these life-friendly conditions existed billions of years before living cells appeared. The findings raise intriguing questions about why the laws of physics seem so well suited to life.
articles.summary: Scientists discover evidence that the universe's fundamental constants are finely balanced in a way that makes the emergence of life possible.

articles.title: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
articles.description: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth.
articles.summary: NASA astronauts aboard SpaceX Crew-12 have successfully returned after 237 days in space, completing a mission spanning over 100 million miles.

articles.title: NASA is searching for hidden caves to build its first Moon base
articles.description: NASA is preparing for humanity’s first Moon base with three investigations that will hunt for underground shelters, uncover hidden ice, and track dangerous conditions on the lunar surface. The findings could reveal how astronauts can survive and thrive on the Moon while laying the groundwork for future journeys to Mars.
articles.summary: NASA is investigating underground lunar caves to serve as shelters for humanity's first Moon base, leveraging natural protection from radiation and temperature extremes. This groundbreaking approach could enable sustainable long-term human presence on the lunar surface.

articles.title: 2 spacecraft in orbit and 8 more coming soon: Varda has big plans for in-space manufacturing
articles.description: Reentry provider Varda Space Industries is currently flying two spacecraft in Earth orbit and has eight more missions planned in the next year.
articles.summary: Varda Space Industries is advancing in-space manufacturing with two operational spacecraft and eight additional missions planned, pioneering a new frontier in commercial space activities. This expansion demonstrates the growing viability of manufacturing beyond Earth's gravity.

articles.title: Physics Nobel highlights Antarctica’s role in exploring the cosmos
articles.description: For more than a century, scientists have treated Antarctica’s environments as windows into worlds beyond Earth.
articles.summary: Antarctica's unique environment has become a vital window for exploring the cosmos, as highlighted by recent Nobel Prize recognition of its role in cosmological discoveries. This remote continent enables groundbreaking astronomical research impossible elsewhere on Earth.

articles.title: Mingarelli elected a new fellow of the American Physical Society
articles.description: Yale physicist Chiara Mingarelli was cited for contributions in pulsar timing array theory and gravitational-wave astrophysics.
articles.summary: Yale physicist Chiara Mingarelli was elected a fellow of the American Physical Society for her contributions to pulsar timing array theory and gravitational-wave research, recognizing groundbreaking work in detecting cosmic gravitational waves.

articles.title: To Win A Nobel Prize, Go To The Ends Of The Earth
articles.description: Neutrinos are persnickety particles. We couldn't really detect neutrinos from deep space until Francis Halzen had a brilliant, Nobel Prize-winning idea.
articles.summary: Physicist Francis Halzen's visionary IceCube experiment in Antarctica revolutionized neutrino detection from deep space, leading to Nobel Prize-winning breakthroughs in understanding the universe's most elusive particles.

articles.title: World Space Week 2026: How the ‘Rocket Revolution’ is changing the cost, speed and future of space travel
articles.description: World Space Week 2026 promises an exciting celebration from October 4 to 10, themed 'Rocket Revolution.' This year's spotlight is on how advancements in rocket technology are opening up access to space. Reusable rockets are making space exploration more affor…
articles.summary: World Space Week 2026 celebrates the 'Rocket Revolution,' highlighting how rapid advances in launch technology are dramatically reducing costs and accelerating humanity's journey to space.

articles.title: NASA Investigating Large Hole on Moon That May Open Into Enormous Cave
articles.description: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University Beneath its pock-marked, craggy exterior, the Moon is thought to harbor a network of caves and tunnels from its volcanic past. Now, NASA has selected a mission to go investigate a promising window into our space rock’s subte…
articles.summary: NASA discovers and investigates a large lunar pit that may be an entrance to an extensive network of cave systems beneath the Moon's surface, offering exciting insights into lunar geology and potential resources.

articles.title: Mars’s oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
articles.description: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express, in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars’s most curious cloud.
articles.summary: ESA's Mars Express combined with advanced meteorological modeling reveals Mars's unique atmospheric cloud formations in unprecedented detail. Scientists continue uncovering the Red Planet's atmospheric mysteries.

articles.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
articles.description:
Image:
			
Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.
As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge.
The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes from stars smaller, older, and cooler than the massive blue stars that dot the galaxy’s outer disc. These tightly packed stars orbit a supermassive black hole containing millions of times the Sun’s mass. Scientists have found signs that this black hole is actively growing, drawing gas inward with its gravitational pull.
With a flat, starry disc and diffusely glowing centre, NGC 4698 looks a lot like a typical spiral galaxy — but this galaxy is far from normal. NGC 4698 is one of only a few known spiral galaxies with a bulge that extends out from the disc at a right angle. The elongation is faintly visible in this Hubble image, which shows the ghostly glow of the starry bulge peeking above and below the dusty disc. What’s more, the stars and gas nearest the galaxy’s centre rotate perpendicular to the rest of the disc.
What could cause a galaxy to be so out of sync? Astronomers have found that the culprit likely lies outside the galaxy. If NGC 4698 funneled in gas from an outside source, the newly collected gas could have formed a disc of gas and stars in the galaxy’s centre, at an angle relative to the rest of the disc. Some observations suggest that this galaxy once experienced a minor galactic merger, as evidenced by a short ‘tail’ of hydrogen streaming from one side of the galaxy.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#18103; PI: Thilker) focusing on galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.
[Image Description: A spiral galaxy viewed at an angle, with a bright central bulge and winding spiral arms. The arms form a ring around the galaxy, without appearing to reach its centre. Prominent red-brown dust lanes weave through the arms, which are also dotted with bright blue and reddish regions of star formation. The galaxy is set against a dark background scattered with stars and faint distant galaxies.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: Hubble Space Telescope captures a spiral galaxy with unusual internal dynamics despite its serene appearance. The observation reveals hidden complexity in galactic structure and rotation.

articles.title: A Red Dwarf is Taking its Time Eating a Brown Dwarf
articles.description: Astronomers detected an unusual triangular light curve about 300 light years away. They were searching for Black Widow Binaries, where a dense neutron star eats its companion. But they found something different: an M dwarf slowly eating its binary companion brown dwarf.
articles.summary: Astronomers detect an unusual triangular light curve from a red dwarf system 300 light-years away, revealing a rare accretion event. This discovery provides insights into binary stellar dynamics.

articles.title: Tiny Gold Nanogaps Could Crack the Chirality Puzzle
articles.description:
Looking for biosignatures across the solar system requires looking for asymmetry. Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are famously either “left-handed” (L) or “right-handed” (D). We know abiotic processes (i.e. those that create amino acids but don’t involve life) create a 50/50 mixture of the two types, which is called a racemic mixture. But life as we know it almost exclusively relies on left-handed amino acids to fold proteins and right-handed ones to construct nucleic acids. So if we find an imbalance in the types of amino acids we analyze from somewhere in the solar system, it's a good indication that life is behind that imbalance.

Differentiating between the two “chiralities”, as they’re called, is possible, but typically requires advanced equipment and chemical disposables that make them burdensome for spaceflight applications. But a new paper in Nature Communications from researchers led by Takahito Ohshiro and Masateru Taniguchi of Osaka University offers an alternative - a solid-state quantum tunneling sensor that can read the chirality of a single amino acid molecule using basically just some gold wire.
articles.summary: Researchers propose using gold nanogaps to detect chirality signatures in the search for biosignatures across the solar system. This innovative technology could revolutionize our ability to identify life-supporting chemistry.

articles.title: Hubble Spots a Suspected Second-Generation Planet
articles.description: Diligent sleuthing by astronomers has broken open a cold case in the data archive of NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope. In a study published Monday in Nature Astronomy, researchers report uncovering a surprising chemical clue that indicates the white dwarf star HS 0209+0832 may host a second-generation planet.
articles.summary: Hubble Space Telescope data reveals a suspected second-generation planet, solving a decades-old astronomical mystery. This discovery expands our understanding of planetary formation mechanisms.
